sentences.text:
The case of the prosecution in nutshell is that on 24.04.2005 at about 10:00 AM at G.B.S.S. School,
Mangolpuri, Delhi, both the accused persons namely Bijender and Devender agreed/ conspired that instead of accused Devender, the other accused Bijender shall be appearing in the said exam of Assistant Teacher after impersonating as accused Devender.

Further, in pursuance of the said conspiracy, on the above mentioned date and time, accused Bijender fraudulently entered the Examination Centre and induced the Invigilator to treat him as the actual candidate.

Also on the abovesaid date, time and place, accused Bijender had placed his forged signatures (while impersonating) on the attendance sheet, admit card and answer sheet, with a intent that such forged signatures shall be used for the purpose of cheating the invigilator.
On the said allegations, the present FIR was registered for the commission of the offences under Section 419/420/468/471/120B IPC.
FIR No. 262/2005 State Vs. Bijender Singh & Anr. Page No. 2 of 23 Dated: 12.11.2024 2.

The investigation into the matter was conducted and upon completion of investigation,
chargesheet was filed against accused Bijender Singh S/o Sh. Mahender Singh and accused Devender Kumar @ Bhallu S/o Sh. Zile Singh for the commission of the offences u/s 419/420/468/471/120B IPC.
3. The cognizance for the offences u/s 419/420/468/471/120B was taken on 20.08.2008 and the accused persons were summoned.
Upon appearance of the accused persons, the compliance of Section 207 CrPC was carried out.

4. The material on record prima facie disclosed the commission of offences u/s 419/420/465/468/120B IPC, thus, the charges were accordingly framed upon both the accused persons on 11.11.2011 to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
Hence, this Court conducted trial.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS 24.

Before embarking to determine the innocence/guilt of the accused in the present case, it would be prudent to discuss the legal standards required to be met by both the sides and it would be prudent to re-produce the relevant sections invoked in the present case.
25. Section 420 IPC provides for the offence of cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property.
Simple cheating is punishable u/s 417 IPC.

But where there is delivery or destruction of any property or alteration or destruction of any valuable security resulting from the act of person deceiving, the same falls under the ambit of section 420.

It reads as under:
"S.420. Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property.--Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or FIR No. 262/2005 State Vs. Bijender Singh & Anr. Page No. 13 of 23 Dated: 12.11.2024 destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine"
It should also be noted that accused should have dishonest intention to cheat right at the time of making the promise or representation.
If he does not have any such intention at the very outset and if he subsequently fails to fulfill the said promise

,
then he cannot be convicted for the offence punishable u/s 420 IPC.
Reference can be taken from the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Hira Lal Hari Lal vs. CBI (2003) 5 SCC 257.

Mere deceit is not sufficient to prove the offence.
The effect of fraudulent or dishonest act must be such that it induces the person deceived to deliver the property or to do something.

"Dishonestly" is defined u/s 24 IPC as "who ever does anything with an intention to causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another person, is said to do that thing dishonestly".
26.On the issue of inducement, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Rajesh Bajaj v. State NCT of Delhi and others AIR 1999 SC 1216 has held that the crux of the postulate is the intention of the person who induces the victim of his representation and not the nature of the transaction which could become decisive in discerning where there was the commission of an offence or not.

sentences.text: Section 468 IPC deals with the offence of forgery committed for the purpose of cheating.
Forgery is defined in section 463 IPC as the making of a false document or false electronic record with any of intentions mentioned therein.

Section 463 reads as under:
"Whoever makes any false documents or false electronic record or part of a document or electronic record, with intent to cause damage or injury, to the public or to any person, or to support any claim or title, or to cause any person to part with property,
or to enter into any express or implied contract, or with intent to commit fraud or that fraud may be committed, commits forgery."

28.Now, the prosecution was under obligation to establish that the accused Bijender has conspired with co-accused Devender (Proceedings abated) to induce the Invigilator on 24.04.2005 for taking the exam of Assistant Teacher at G.B.S.S. School, Mangolpuri, Delhi.

Further, the prosecution was under obligation to establish that the accused Bijender has placed his forged signatures on the Attendance Sheet, Admit Card as well as the Answersheet with an intent to use such forged signatures as genuine.
29. It is essential to prove that the individuals involved had a meeting of mind or intended to co-operate for pursuing a common goal.
The prosecution had to establish the factum of conspiracy between both the accused persons.
The foundation of criminal conspiracy is the existence of an agreement between two or more individuals.

crucial witnesses of the prosecution were PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3.

The various contradictions and inconsistencies within the testimonies of the said witnesses are as follows:
a) As per PW-1, the DSSSB/ Police Officials and some other persons had brought a boy to his office at the fag FIR No. 262/2005 State Vs. Bijender Singh & Anr. Page No. 16 of 23 Dated: 12.11.2024 end of the exam, meaning thereby that the said witness was never the part of the alleged checking stated to have been conducted by PW-2 and PW-3.

b) As per PW-1, no documents were seized from the candidate in his presence,
meaning thereby that the Ex.
PW1/C (the seizure memo of the Admit Card dated 24.04.2005) which is stated to be bearing the signatures of PW-1 at point D, is doubtful as the said witness has clearly negated the seizure of any document in his presence.

c) On the similar lines, the Ex. PW1/G (i.e. the seizure memo of the Voter I Card), which is stated to be bearing the signatures of PW-1 at point A,is doubtful as the said witness has clearly negated the seizure of any document in his presence.

d) PW-1 has submitted that his signatures were obtained on the arrest memo i.e. Ex. PW1/H, late in the evening, while the time of the arrest of accused Bijender is stated to be 03:00 pm on 24.04.2005.

Now, by any stretch of imagination 03:00 PM cannot be considered as a late evening and as admitted the signatures of the PW-1 were obtained on the arrest memo, meaning thereby that the accused was never arrested in his presence which justifies the subsequent obtainment of the signatures of PW-1 on the arrest memo i.e. Ex. PW1/H.

e) As per PW-1, no answersheet, question booklet and the Admit Card were seized in his presence while as per seizure memo (Ex. PW1/C), PW-1 is stated to be the FIR No. 262/2005 State Vs.

However, on 24.04.2005, despite the factum of registration of the FIR on the said day itself, there is no seizure memo in respect of the said original documents/ the question paper/ the FIR No. 262/2005 State Vs. Bijender Singh & Anr. Page No. 19 of 23 Dated: 12.11.2024 answersheet on the said day.
Surprisingly, there is a seizure memo which is Ex. PW11/D dated 02.05.2005 vide which a photocopy of the answersheet was stated to be seized.

Further, there is a seizure memo which is Ex. PW9/A dated 17.05.2005, as per which the answersheet bearing no. 1005075 and a question-cum-answer booklet No. 15072 (both in original)
were stated to be seized vide the said seizure memo.

FORENSIC/ SCIENTIFIC EVIDENCE 34.FSL
Report is in the nature of evidence of hand writing expert which is admissible in evidence under Section 45 of the Indian Evidence Act.
It is admissible per se u/s 293 Cr.P.C. also and can be used as evidence during the course of trial without it being formally proved.

35. However, it is settled proposition of law that before acting upon the opinion of the hand-writing expert, prudence requires that the court must see that such evidence is corroborated by other evidence either direct or circumstantial evidence.
The evidence of an expert is rather a weak piece of evidence, and, therefore, should not be considered as "conclusive" poof in the absence of any independent and reliable corroboration.

At this stage, reference can be taken from the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Magan Bihari Vs. State of Punjab (1977) 2 SCC 210,
wherein while dealing with the evidence of a handwriting expert, the Apex Court opined that "...........
We think

There is a profusion of precedential authority which hold that it is unsafe to base a conviction solely on expert opinion without substantial corroboration.
This rule has been universally acted upon and it has almost become a rule of law.

It was held by this Court in Ram Chandra Vs. State of U.P. AIR 1957 SC 381 that it is unsafe to treat expert handwriting opinion as sufficient basis for conviction, but it may be relied upon when supported by other items of internal and external evidence.

sentences.text: , in the instant case, the FSL Report is Ex. PW12/A and perusal of the same reflects that it bears an observation "it has not been possible to express any opinion on the rest of the items on the basis of the material at hand".

is pertinent to note that as per the observation of the handwriting expert, the questioned signatures do not match with the specimen signatures/ handwriting of the accused Devender.

Meaning thereby, the FSL Report could not suggest the link of accused Bijender with the present case.
38. Hence, in view of the discussion made hereinabove, the Court is of the view that the prosecution has miserably failed to establish the guilt of accused Bijender beyond reasonable doubt.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
The essential ingredients to attract section 420 IPC are:
 Cheating;
 Dishonest inducement to deliver property or to make, alter or destroy any valuable security or anything which is sealed or is capable of being converted into a valuable security; and  Mens rea of the accused at the time of making the inducement.
It should also be noted that accused should have dishonest intention to cheat right at the time of making the promise or representation.
If he does not have any such intention at the very outset and if he subsequently fails to fulfill the said promise
,
then he cannot be convicted for the offence punishable u/s 420 IPC.
Reference can be taken from the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Hira Lal Hari Lal vs. CBI (2003) 5 SCC 257.
A fraudulent or dishonest inducement is an essential ingredient of the offence.
A person who dishonestly induces another person to deliver any property is liable for the offence of cheating.

Mere deceit is not sufficient to prove the offence.
The effect of fraudulent or dishonest act must be such that it induces the person deceived to deliver the property or to do something.
